articles.title: The Wall That Could Not Stand
articles.dek: Two enemy nations once buried the hatchet with a treaty. Paul says Christ did something far more radical to end an older, deeper war.
articles.quote: Jesus didn't broker a truce between two old enemies. He built a brand-new family that had never existed until the cross made it possible.
articles.body:
On May 9, 1950, a French foreign minister named Robert Schuman stood before reporters in Paris and proposed something that sounded almost absurd. France and Germany had fought three wars in eighty years. Millions of their young men lay buried because of it. Schuman's plan for lasting peace was not another treaty of promises, which everyone knew could be broken. It was to pool the two nations' coal and steel production — the very raw materials both countries used to build tanks, artillery, and warships — under one shared authority. If the weapons-making itself belonged to both nations together, he reasoned, war between them would become, in his own words, "not merely unthinkable, but materially impossible." It worked. That plan became the seed of what is now the European Union. Two of history's bitterest enemies didn't just agree to stop fighting. They built something new together that neither had ever been on its own.

Paul had a much older, much deeper wall in mind when he wrote to the church in Ephesus — and he wasn't speaking only in metaphor. In the Jerusalem temple of his day stood an actual stone barrier, about four and a half feet high, called the soreg. It ran around the inner courts, and at intervals, warning signs were carved into it in Greek and Latin. One of those very inscriptions was unearthed by archaeologists in 1871 and can still be read today in a museum. It warns that no foreigner may pass beyond the barrier into the sanctuary, and that anyone who does will have himself to thank for the death that follows. That was not a metaphor for exclusion. It was carved in stone, backed by Rome's own permission to execute trespassers on sight.

That wall stood for something far bigger than architecture. For centuries, Jew and Gentile had been kept apart — not by preference, but by law, by circumcision, by food rules and feast days and a history of hostility so old that neither side remembered exactly when the wall of custom first went up. Paul reminds his readers that Gentiles were once "separate from Christ, excluded from citizenship in Israel and foreigners to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world" (Eph 2:12). And then, in the very next breath, he says something happened.

"For he himself is our peace, who has made the two groups one and has destroyed the barrier, the dividing wall of hostility, by setting aside in his flesh the law with its commands and regulations. His purpose was to create in himself one new humanity out of the two, thus making peace, and in one body to reconcile both of them to God through the cross, by which he put to death their hostility." (Eph 2:14–16, NIV)

Read that slowly, because it's easy to slide past the most surprising word in it: not "reconciled," not "united," but created. Schuman's plan, for all its brilliance, still left France as France and Germany as Germany — two nations who agreed to cooperate. Notice that Paul says Christ did something more radical than a treaty. He didn't simply get two hostile groups to tolerate one another. He made "one new humanity out of the two" (v. 15) — a third thing that had never existed before the cross. Not Jew-plus-Gentile living politely side by side under a new set of rules. Something genuinely, freshly new.

And notice what it cost to make it. Schuman's peace was signed with ink at a press conference. This peace was made "in his flesh" (v. 14) and "through the cross" (v. 16). Paul says Christ "put to death their hostility" — and the death that ended it was his own. The wall didn't come down because two sides finally negotiated better terms. It came down because someone stepped into the gap between them and absorbed the full cost of tearing it out.

Here's the detail worth sitting with longest. That warning stone at the temple existed for one purpose: to keep Gentiles out, to protect sacred space from anyone who wasn't the right kind of person, on pain of death. But look at what Paul says happens to those very people just a few verses later: "you are no longer foreigners and strangers, but fellow citizens with God's people and also members of his household... In him the whole building is joined together and rises to become a holy temple in the Lord. And in him you also are being built together to become a dwelling in which God lives by his Spirit" (Eph 2:19–22). The people the old wall was built to keep away from God's house are now, in Christ, the very stones that make up God's house. Not tolerated at the edge of the courtyard. Built into the structure itself, with Jesus as "the chief cornerstone" (v. 20) — the stone every other stone lines up against.

Most of us are guarding a smaller version of that wall somewhere. Maybe it's a relative you've stopped speaking to. Maybe it's the coworker, the in-law, or the old friend whose politics or past mistakes make peace feel impossible. Maybe it's simply the quiet, unspoken conviction that certain people — because of where they come from, what they've done, or what was done to them — belong on the far side of a line, and you belong on the near side of it.

It's worth asking: if two nations that had buried millions of their own sons in wars against each other could end up sharing a currency and a parliament within a lifetime, what wall are you still guarding that Christ has already torn down at the cross two thousand years ago? Paul isn't handing you a strategy for managing your enemies more gracefully. He's telling you the hostility itself has already been executed — his word, not a softer one — and that whatever new "us" Christ wants to build out of your old "us versus them" is worth reaching for now, not someday.

So here is something to carry with you this week: you are not merely permitted into God's house, standing politely near the door, grateful to have been let in. You are being built into it, fitted stone by stone into something alive. If Christ could take the very people a temple wall was built to keep out and turn them into living stones of a new temple, he can do something with whatever wall you are facing today — in your family, your church, your own history. Start smaller than a treaty between nations. Send the message you've been avoiding. Make the call you've been putting off. Let the wall you've been guarding be the next one that comes down.

articles.title: The God Who Doesn't Need a Ride
articles.dek: Babylon's gods had to be loaded onto tired animals just to be moved. Isaiah says the real God carries the load — and never puts it down.
articles.quote: The idols of Babylon had to be carried. The God of Israel does the carrying.
articles.illustration: whale calves riding their mother's slipstream
articles.body:
Marine biologists tracking humpback and right whales noticed something strange in the data. Calves swimming beside their mothers were barely working. Their tail beats were slower, their oxygen use lower, their whole bodies riding an invisible cushion of water that the mother's massive frame pushed ahead of her. It's called echelon swimming: the calf tucks in just behind and slightly to the side of mom, catching her slipstream the way a cyclist drafts behind another rider. She does the work of pushing through the ocean. The calf simply comes along, carried by a current its mother is making just for it, for months, until it's strong enough to make its own way.

Isaiah gives us a picture that runs the opposite direction — and it's one of the most vivid scenes in the whole book. Babylon is about to fall, and its gods are on the move. "Bel bows down, Nebo stoops low," Isaiah writes; "their idols are borne by beasts of burden. The images that are carried about are burdensome, a burden for the weary animal" (Isa 46:1). Picture it: the priests of Babylon, in a panic, are loading their gold and silver gods onto the backs of oxen and mules to save them from the invading Persian army. These are supposed to be the powers that rule the universe. And they can't even get down the street without an animal's back underneath them. The very statues meant to protect the city have to be rescued like furniture.

Isaiah doesn't let the irony pass quietly. "They stoop and bow down together; unable to rescue the burden, they themselves go off into captivity" (Isa 46:2). The gods can't save the city. They can't even save themselves. They are, in the end, just cargo — dead weight that living creatures have to haul.

Then, in the very next breath, God turns to his own people and draws the sharpest possible contrast.

"Listen to me, you descendants of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, you whom I have upheld since your birth, and have carried since you were born. Even to your old age and gray hairs I am he, I am he who will sustain you. I have made you and I will carry you; I will sustain you and I will rescue you." (Isa 46:3–4, NIV)

Notice the verb Isaiah reaches for on both sides of this picture. The idols are carried — helplessly, by tired animals, toward exile. God's people are carried too — but by God himself, from birth all the way to gray hair. Same word, in the Hebrew, doing two completely different jobs. One kind of carrying is a burden dragging something down. The other is a Father lifting something up.

Here's what's easy to miss on a first read: this isn't just a promise for the young or the newly rescued. "Even to your old age and gray hairs I am he." A whale calf eventually grows strong enough to swim on its own; the slipstream is a season, not a lifetime. But God specifically names the far end of life — the years when strength fades, when a person can least carry their own weight — and says that's exactly where he keeps carrying. He doesn't carry us until we're capable and then step back. He carries us because he made us, and that doesn't expire.

It's worth sitting with why Isaiah chose this particular contrast. Babylon's gods needed to be carried because they were never alive to begin with — gold and wood have no strength of their own; they only ever borrow it from whoever hauls them around. But it's also worth asking what we quietly ask people, and even ourselves, to carry that was never meant to be carried. A reputation that has to be constantly propped up. A plan we keep hauling forward on our own back long after it's stopped working. A worry we drag from room to room like a suitcase we can't put down. None of that is evil, exactly — it's just exhausting, the way hoisting a lifeless idol onto a mule is exhausting. It takes something out of the carrier and gives nothing back.

God is offering something different in these verses, and he's specific about it: he made us, so he'll carry us; he'll sustain us, so he'll also rescue us. Four verbs, all pointed the same direction — toward us, not away from us. This is a relational promise before it's anything else. It's the difference between a god you have to prop up with your own strength and a God who says, plainly, you are the one being carried here, not me.

There's a tender, almost domestic image tucked into verse 3 that's easy to rush past: "you whom I have upheld since your birth." The Hebrew pictures something closer to a father lifting a newborn, or an old man being helped along by a steady arm. It's not the language of a distant sovereign issuing decrees from a throne. It's the language of someone who has been present, hands-on, since the very first day — the way a mother whale doesn't just watch her calf swim, she reshapes the water itself so the calf can keep up.

So here's something worth carrying into this week, gently: notice what you're currently hauling that was never meant to be yours to lift. Maybe it's an old failure you keep dragging behind you. Maybe it's a family expectation, or a fear about tomorrow, or a version of yourself you're exhausted from propping up in front of other people. Isaiah's picture invites you to set it down — not because it doesn't matter, but because you were never built to be the one doing the carrying. That's not a burden God hands you. That's a burden God takes.

articles.title: Remember Me, Too
articles.dek: A global hotel chain once solved the problem of guests feeling forgotten. A psalmist solved it first — by whispering two words in the middle of a nation's anthem.
articles.quote: In the middle of the crowd's great anthem, God still bends down to hear one small voice say, 'Remember me.'
articles.body:
In the early 1990s, the Ritz-Carlton Hotel Company noticed a strange problem hiding inside its own success. The brand was growing fast — new hotels opening on nearly every continent — but the bigger it got, the more guests complained of the very same quiet ache: nobody here knows me. A traveler might mention, once, in passing, that she liked a firmer pillow, or that he was allergic to shellfish, or that this Tuesday happened to be her late husband's birthday. A kind employee would note it, help her that one time, and then she'd fly home. Next trip, different city, different staff — and she was a stranger again.

So the company built something almost embarrassingly simple: a shared notebook. Every employee, from housekeeping to the front desk, was trained to write down anything a guest revealed about themselves and feed it into one database every Ritz-Carlton on earth could read. A guest checking into a hotel in Bali could be greeted with the same pillow, the same care, even the same small joke, they'd shared with a stranger in Singapore eight months before. The problem the company solved wasn't really service. It was memory. It kept guests from disappearing into the crowd of a growing empire.

Psalm 106 opens with a sound the size of a nation. "Praise the LORD," it begins — hallelu-Yah — and forty-eight verses later, it will end the very same way. In between comes a sweeping retelling of Israel's history: the Red Sea splitting, the wilderness grumbling, decades of a people forgetting God's wonders almost as fast as he performed them, and God remaining stubbornly faithful anyway. This is a psalm built for a crowd — priests, farmers, mothers with children on their hips — all lifting one collective voice over a long, complicated story. It speaks of "his people," "his chosen ones," "his nation." Centuries of faces. One song.

And then, without warning, right in the middle of all that collective praising, one voice breaks off from the chorus.

"Remember me, LORD, when you show favor to your people, come to my aid when you save them, that I may enjoy the prosperity of your chosen ones, that I may share in the joy of your nation, that I may join your inheritance in giving praise." (Psalm 106:4–5, NIV)

Notice what the psalmist does not pray. He doesn't ask God to treat him differently from everyone else, doesn't request a private blessing that skips the line. Every verb points back to the group: "when you show favor to your people," "come to my aid when you save them." He isn't stepping out of the crowd's song. He's asking to be found inside it. It's worth asking why a single "remember me" feels almost like an interruption in a psalm built for a nation. Because it is — and that's the whole point. In the middle of retelling four centuries of a people's history, one person plants a small flag and says: don't let me become a statistic in this story. Let me be a name.

Here's the fresh part, the thing easy to miss on a quick read: the psalmist isn't asking to enjoy God's blessing instead of his people, or apart from them. Look at what he actually wants — to share the prosperity of "your chosen ones," the joy of "your nation," a place in "your inheritance." His personal plea and the community's story aren't competing. He wants his one small life woven into the larger one, not carved out from it. That's a different shape of prayer than most of us default to. We tend to swing between "bless me" and "bless everyone," as if personal and communal are two separate lanes. The psalmist prays them as one sentence.

For a Filipino reader, this lands somewhere familiar. So much of life here is lived in the plural — the barangay, the extended clan, the parish, the whole neighborhood arriving for a fiesta or a wake. There's real beauty in that, and real pressure too: a sense that your personal ache should quietly wait its turn behind the family's, the church's, the nation's bigger story. Psalm 106 says you don't have to choose. You can rejoice at your kapatid's wedding and still whisper, remember me too, Lord, in what I'm carrying this year. You can thank God for your family's harvest and still bring him the ache of the son or daughter working overseas, far from the table. The individual prayer doesn't shrink the communal one. It fits inside it, the way a single thread still belongs to the whole weave.

Unlike the Ritz-Carlton, which needed years and real money to build a system that could remember one guest among millions, God never had to build anything. He already keeps the record. The psalmist isn't discovering new technology; he's simply trusting the character already announced in verse one — "he is good; his love endures forever" (Psalm 106:1). That's the ground his whole request stands on. Not proof. Not a database. Just the settled trust that the God who is writing history at the scale of nations still has room in the sentence for one more name.

So here's something small to carry today. However crowded your season feels — however many people God seems to be attending to before he gets around to you — you're allowed to pray exactly what this ancient voice prayed, right in the middle of everyone else's story. Two words are enough. Remember me. Not instead of your people. Alongside them. He already has the notebook open, and your page has been there the whole time.

articles.title: The Cardigan That Earned $20 Million
articles.dek: A quiet man in a sweater walked into a hostile Senate hearing with nothing but warmth — and Solomon could have told the senators exactly why it worked.
articles.quote: The proverb doesn't measure your table by its size. It measures the temperature of the room.
articles.body:
On May 1, 1969, a mild-mannered television host in a hand-knit cardigan sat down in front of the United States Senate Subcommittee on Communications and asked for six minutes. Congress was weighing a proposal to cut federal funding for public television in half, from $20 million to $10 million, at a time when the country had far bigger things fighting for its money — a war overseas, inflation at home, a long list of programs all claiming to matter most. The subcommittee chairman, Senator John Pastore, was a famously impatient man, known for cutting witnesses off mid-sentence when they wasted his time, and he had already sat through hours of dry testimony that day. He told the witness bluntly: you have six minutes. The witness was Fred Rogers.

Rogers did not bring charts. He did not bring lobbyists or statistics about viewership. He simply talked, in that same unhurried voice millions of children already knew, about what his program actually did. He talked about helping a child understand anger without hitting a sibling or a pet. He talked about self-worth, about a child's need to hear, in plain words, that someone cared. Then, almost shyly, he asked if he could recite the words to a song he had written called "What Do You Do with the Mad That You Feel?" Pastore, who moments earlier had been checking his watch, said yes. Rogers recited it slowly, the way he spoke to a camera every morning. When he finished, the room was silent. Pastore, visibly moved, said, "I think it's wonderful. Look, I've been up here for the last two days, and I've listened to a lot of testimony. This is the first time I've had goosebumps." Then he added the line that mattered most for public television's future: "It looks like you just earned your twenty million dollars."

Six minutes. No slides. No spectacle. A man in a cardigan, two puppets, a trolley, and a fish tank had, for years, been quietly out-competing networks with bigger budgets and flashier sets, because he offered something they didn't: unhurried, undivided warmth. His entire studio, by television standards, was almost embarrassingly plain — a painted backdrop, a handful of puppets he voiced himself, no laugh track, no special effects. And yet in a hearing room built for political combat, the gentlest, plainest thing in the building was what won the argument.

Solomon was writing about rooms like that one, three thousand years before it happened. Proverbs 15 spends its early verses at the level of a household — moods at the dinner table, the difference between a home that feels like a feast and one that feels like a funeral, even when the same food is on both tables. "A happy heart makes the face cheerful," he writes, "but heartache crushes the spirit" (Proverbs 15:13). Two verses later: "All the days of the oppressed are wretched, but the cheerful heart has a continual feast" (Proverbs 15:15). And then Solomon lands the point with a single, unforgettable picture of two dinner tables.

Better a small serving of vegetables with love than a fattened calf with hatred. — Proverbs 15:17 (NIV)

Read that verse slowly and notice what Solomon is not saying. He isn't saying money is bad, or that abundance is a trap, or that you should feel guilty for wanting a good meal. A fattened calf was no small thing in the ancient world — it meant an animal deliberately grain-fed and set aside months in advance for a wedding, a homecoming, or a king's table. It's the same fattened calf the father slaughters for his returning son in Jesus' famous parable. Solomon isn't against the calf. He's against what's sitting at the table with it: hatred, strife, a home where the food is rich but the air is cold.

Here's the fresh angle worth sitting with: the proverb doesn't measure your table by its size. It measures the temperature of the room. That's exactly what happened in that Senate hearing room. Every other witness that year probably came with bigger asks, bigger numbers, bigger production values. Rogers came with something closer to the vegetables — small, plain, unglamorous by comparison. And it fed that room more than any budget line item could have, because it carried love where everything else in the building carried leverage.

It's worth asking where you've been quietly waiting for the fattened calf before you'll bring the love. Waiting for the promotion before you celebrate. Waiting for the big reunion, the special occasion, the debt-free year, before the table finally feels warm. Solomon is telling you the order is backward. The cheerful heart doesn't wait for a continual feast to show up — it is the continual feast, served over whatever is actually on the table tonight: rice and one ulam, a modest carinderia meal shared after a long shift, a phone call instead of a visit you can't afford yet.

Think about how many homes get this backward without ever meaning to. A family saves for months for one lavish fiesta table, sets it beautifully, and spends the whole meal on edge — old arguments resurfacing, comparisons being made, everyone performing for relatives instead of actually seeing them. Meanwhile another family, two streets over, is eating instant noodles standing up in a small kitchen, laughing about something that happened at work, genuinely glad to be near each other. Solomon has already told us which of those two tables is the feast. It was never about what got served.

This is where the gospel quietly stands behind Solomon's proverb. Grace has never worked by first upgrading the meal. It reaches whoever is at the table exactly as they are — tired, ordinary, empty-handed — and it's the love at the center, not the portion size, that turns a plate of vegetables into something that actually satisfies. Jesus fed crowds with barley loaves a boy happened to be carrying, and he broke bread for his closest friends the night before he died using nothing more than what was already on the table. He never once waited for a better meal to make his point. He kept showing up to ordinary tables and making them holy by simply being present at them, fully, in love. That's the same reason a six-minute testimony in a cardigan outlasted every polished argument in that hearing room. Love travels lighter than we think, and it arrives further than money ever does.

So here is something to actually do with this, today. Look at whatever table is in front of you tonight — literal or otherwise. Don't wait to make it bigger before you make it warm. Ask one real question and actually listen to the answer. Say the plain sentence Rogers built an entire career on: I'm glad you're here. You don't need a bigger table to have a continual feast. You just need a warmer room — and that part, Solomon says, has always been within reach.
